title: Choosing an Own-Stay Home: Affordability, Intent and the 85% Rule
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #282 | CONSIDERATIONS FOR OWN-STAY PROPERTY
excerpt: How to decide when a home is worth buying for stability and daily life, while preserving a workable exit if circumstances change.
takeaways: Separate the purpose of a home from the purpose of an investment before comparing properties.
Sean's 85% rule asks whether realistic market rent could cover roughly 85% of the mortgage if you later need to move.
Savings, career clarity, protection and long-term familiarity with the location matter more than pressure to own.

sections.heading: Start with the life the home must support
paragraphs: An own-stay purchase is allowed to deliver value that cannot be measured as rental yield. Stability, control over the space and the freedom to design around daily routines can justify spending money. The mistake is treating those emotional benefits as proof that any dream home is affordable or easy to exit.

Sean recommends establishing the intent first, then reviewing savings, career stability, insurance or other protection, and family responsibilities. A buyer who already knows and repeatedly chooses a location is making a more informed decision than someone moving far away simply to obtain a preferred housing type.

sections.heading: Use rent as an exit test
paragraphs: Sean's 85% rule is a practical own-stay heuristic: if the area's realistic rent can cover about 85% of the proposed monthly mortgage, a future move may be less painful. The rent is not expected to make the home a perfect investment; it creates a buffer by covering much of the financing cost while circumstances change.

This matters because jobs, relationships and care needs can move faster than a property. A centrally located home with established rental demand gives the owner another option. A highly personalised home in a distant, thinly traded location can be harder to rent, harder to sell and expensive to hold while renting somewhere else.

sections.heading: Pay consciously for certainty
paragraphs: Once the financial base and exit are credible, the remaining question is whether the buyer values the certainty enough to pay for it. Ownership removes the risk of a landlord reclaiming the home at an inconvenient time and lets the resident shape the space around work, rest and family.

Renovation and lifestyle upgrades should be treated honestly as spending for use and enjoyment. They may improve the owner's life without returning their full cost at resale. A sound decision recognises both sides: the home can be an intentional expense, and the mortgage still has to leave room for savings and unexpected change.

closing: Buy an own-stay home when the location, finances and need for stability align—and when a realistic rental exit keeps one future change from becoming a crisis.
sourceNote: Based on the full public English captions and published episode notes for Asking Sean #282. The 85% rule is Sean's personal heuristic, not a lending standard; verify affordability and current rents independently.
